viewpoints.claim: Every action with consequences shows the user something changed, as quickly as possible, so they always know what the system is doing.

source.author: Jakob Nielsen
source.work: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design, heuristic #1
source.quote: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.

prefers: Show a visible trace of every state change
Give feedback immediately, or as quickly as possible
Disable and label a control while its action runs
forbids: Submit silently
Change state with no visible trace
Show an action's result only somewhere else

measure.what: Drive an action, then diff DOM or pixels over the next frames: did anything visibly change within 1 s; is there a live region, status text, spinner or busy state?
measure.mustFail: A Save button posts and re-renders identical pixels for 3 s, then updates.
measure.mustPass: Same button disabled with 'Saving…' within 100 ms, then 'Saved' in a status element.

exceptions: Below 0.1 s no special feedback is needed beyond showing the result
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages have few stateful actions beyond a form submit or a subscribe click.

viewpoints.claim: Paint something within 0.1 s; keep the user's flow with a response under 1 s; show a progress indicator for anything longer.

source.author: Jakob Nielsen
source.work: Response Times: The 3 Important Limits (1993)
source.quote: 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously … 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted

prefers: Use a progress indicator for any action over about 1 s
Use a looped indicator for 2–9 s waits
Use a percent-done indicator for 10 s or more
forbids: Leave dead time with no indicator
Show a percent-done bar that lies badly

measure.what: Time from input event to first paint of any change; presence of a progress element, aria-busy, <progress> or role=status update when the wait exceeds 1 s.
measure.mustFail: A click triggers a 2.5 s fetch with no DOM change until the response.
measure.mustPass: Same fetch, spinner or skeleton painted under 400 ms after the click.

exceptions: Laws of UX claims a purposeful delay can raise perceived value — an opinion with no study cited
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages rarely trigger a wait worth a progress indicator.

viewpoints.claim: Write in the words the actor already uses; no internal jargon, error codes or unexplained abbreviations.

source.author: Jakob Nielsen
source.work: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design, heuristic #2
source.quote: The design should speak the users' language. Use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user, rather than internal jargon.

prefers: Use words the user understands without looking them up
Spell acronyms out in full on each page
Write 'for example', not 'eg' or 'ie'
forbids: Show bare error codes
Expose internal entity names
Use unexplained abbreviations

measure.what: Flag bare error codes (e.g. ERR-422, Error 0x…), all-caps acronyms not defined on the page, and Latin abbreviations; whether a term is jargon for this actor needs the journey's actor.
measure.mustFail: 'ERR_VALIDATION_422: payload rejected'.
measure.mustPass: 'Check the email address — it needs an @.'

exceptions: Expert-only tools where the domain term is the users' language — match the user, do not simplify per se

viewpoints.claim: Every interaction has a visible, labelled way out — Cancel, Back, Escape, Undo — so a mistaken action does not trap the user.

source.author: Jakob Nielsen
source.work: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design, heuristic #3
source.quote: Users often perform actions by mistake. They need a clearly marked 'emergency exit' to leave the unwanted action without having to go through an extended process.

prefers: Support Undo and Redo
Show a clear Cancel or close control
Label the exit clearly and make it discoverable
forbids: Open a modal with no close
Build a wizard step with no back
Ship a destructive action with no undo

measure.what: For each role=dialog or modal: a focusable control whose text or aria-label matches close/cancel/back, and Escape dismisses it; for each step past the first in a flow: a back control exists.
measure.mustFail: A dialog whose only button is 'Continue' and which ignores Escape.
measure.mustPass: Same dialog with 'Cancel' and Escape wired.

exceptions: Legally required interstitials — the exit must still be visible, not necessarily free of consequence
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages open a dialog only occasionally, for a cookie or subscribe popup.

viewpoints.claim: Everything on the screen competes with the primary goal; remove what does not serve it so the main action stays visible.

source.author: Jakob Nielsen
source.work: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design, heuristic #8
source.quote: Every extra unit of information in an interface competes with the relevant units of information and diminishes their relative visibility.

prefers: Prioritise content and features that support the primary goal
Keep the primary action in the first viewport
Let the small screen force focus on what matters
forbids: Let decorative elements distract
Let secondary content outweigh the primary action

measure.what: At 360 px: count distinct interactive elements above the fold; whether the journey's primary action is within the first viewport; count of elements sharing the accent colour.
measure.mustFail: At 360 px the 'Continue' button sits below three promo cards and a newsletter box.
measure.mustPass: Same page, 'Continue' in the first viewport.

exceptions: Dense expert dashboards where the irreducible information is large
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Content, dashboards, admin tools and catalogue pages can legitimately carry a large irreducible amount of information (Tesler's law).

viewpoints.claim: The best help is none; when a field needs explaining, put a short hint beside it at the moment it is needed, not on another page.

source.author: Jakob Nielsen
source.work: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design, heuristic #10
source.quote: Whenever possible, present the documentation in context right at the moment that the user requires it.

prefers: Use hint text for help relevant to most users
Keep hint text to one short sentence without full stops
Associate the hint with its input via aria-describedby
forbids: Put help only on a separate page
Put links inside hint text
Write lengthy explanations

measure.what: For inputs with a format expectation (date, postcode, card): a hint associated via aria-describedby and rendered adjacent, same column, within one line-height; hint length in sentences.
measure.mustFail: A date field whose format rules live only in a 'Help' link in the footer.
measure.mustPass: 'For example, 27 3 2007' under the label.

exceptions: Nielsen's own first sentence: it is best if the system needs no additional explanation
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages carry no inputs to hint at; dashboards and catalogue pages carry few.

viewpoints.claim: Links and buttons must look clickable — colour, underline, border or fill — because weak signifiers cost measured time and fixations.

source.author: Kate Moran, NN/g
source.work: Flat UI Elements Attract Less Attention and Cause Uncertainty (2017)
source.quote: 22% more time

prefers: Make links stand out from body text
Make buttons resemble physical buttons with rectangular shapes
Apply consistent treatment throughout the site
Provide signifiers rather than rely on affordances
forbids: Style linked text as static text
Use ghost buttons as the default
Use disabled buttons if avoidable
Rely on a label to say that a control is a control

measure.what: For each a[href], button, [role=button]: computed colour, underline, border and background versus surrounding text; a link matching body colour with no underline and no other differentiator is weak; count disabled buttons.
measure.mustFail: a { color: inherit; text-decoration: none } inside a paragraph.
measure.mustPass: Same link with a distinct hue or an underline.

exceptions: Link position in nav menus or peripheral lists may eliminate the need for underlining (Loranger)
Flat works best with low information density, traditional layouts and high-contrast targets positioned standardly (Moran)

viewpoints.claim: Nothing that is not interactive may look interactive: no underlined or blue static text, no button-shaped badges, no pointer cursor on inert elements.

source.author: Hoa Loranger, NN/g
source.work: Beyond Blue Links: Making Clickable Elements Recognizable (2015)
source.quote: Avoid making non-clickable items (like headings) resemble buttons.

prefers: Reserve link colour and underline for links
Reserve button shape and fill for buttons
forbids: Give static items hyperlink colours
Underline non-interactive text
Make headings or badges resemble buttons

measure.what: Elements with no href, handler, role or tabindex that have cursor: pointer, underline plus link colour, or a button-like box (border-radius, filled background, short centred text).
measure.mustFail: A Premium badge styled exactly like the real buttons.
measure.mustPass: Same badge as a pill with no button colour and no pointer cursor.

viewpoints.claim: Put a control next to the thing it changes and a label next to its field; gaps between groups must exceed gaps within them.

source.author: Marieke McCloskey, NN/g
source.work: Form Design Quick Fix: Group Form Elements Effectively Using White Space (2013)
source.quote: items near each other appear related

prefers: Place labels as close to their fields as possible
Group related fields together
Place related targets close to each other
Put the call to action near the final form fields
forbids: Put a control far from the thing it changes
Separate groups by less space than their members

measure.what: Distance from each label to its own input versus the nearest other input; gap within a fieldset versus gap between fieldsets; distance from last input to the submit button.
measure.mustFail: Left labels 240 px from their inputs, uniform 16 px gaps everywhere.
measure.mustPass: Labels 4 px above inputs, 8 px within groups, 32 px between groups.

exceptions: Left-aligned labels are acceptable if space is constrained and labels are of similar length

viewpoints.claim: Complexity that cannot be removed goes to the system, not the user: default what can be inferred, hide what is rarely needed.

source.author: Larry Tesler, via Jon Yablonski (Laws of UX)
source.work: Tesler's Law — Laws of UX
source.quote: For any system there is a certain amount of complexity which cannot be reduced

prefers: Set billing address equal to shipping by default
Hide Address Line 2 behind an expandable link
Collapse coupon code fields by default
Offer account creation after checkout completion
forbids: Ask for what the system can infer or default
Show rarely used fields by default

measure.what: Count visible required inputs the page could default (no 'same as shipping' control, both address blocks open); presence of autocomplete tokens on address and payment inputs.
measure.mustFail: Two full address forms shown, no 'same as shipping' control.
measure.mustPass: One address form plus a checked 'Billing address is the same' toggle.

exceptions: Tognazzini's counter-view: users resist complexity reduction and attempt harder tasks when systems get simpler
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages take no input to default or hide; dashboards and catalogue pages ask for little.

viewpoints.claim: A page's purpose and controls should be self-evident; nothing on it should raise a question the user must answer before acting.

source.author: Steve Krug
source.work: Don't Make Me Think (2nd ed.), chapter 1 — Krug's First Law of Usability
source.quote: Don't make me think!

prefers: Make the page's purpose obvious at a glance
Make every control self-evident
forbids: Raise a question the user must answer before acting

measure.what: Look at the screen cold: is there anything you have to work out before you can act? The law is the sum of the other entries; a machine measures its symptoms, not the law.

viewpoints.claim: Do not count clicks; make each one an unambiguous choice with clear link text that says where it goes.

source.author: Steve Krug
source.work: Don't Make Me Think, Revisited — chapter 4 (Krug's Second Law of Usability)
source.quote: It doesn't matter how many times I have to click, as long as each click is a mindless, unambiguous choice.

prefers: Write link text that identifies its target
Use breadcrumbs and hub pages for scent
Keep clear labelling with strong information scent
forbids: Count clicks as the metric
Use generic links like 'Click here' or 'Learn more'

measure.what: Count links and buttons whose text is generic ('Click here', 'Learn more', 'Read more', bare 'Next') or duplicates another link's text with a different target; do not measure path length.
measure.mustFail: Three cards each with a 'Learn more' link to different pages.
measure.mustPass: 'See pricing', 'Read the security policy', 'Compare plans'.

exceptions: Fewer clicks matter more when the same path is drilled repeatedly or pages take long to load (Krug)
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Dashboards, admin tools and transaction flows lean on a small set of known controls rather than open link navigation.

viewpoints.claim: Design for scanning, not reading: headings that out-rank body text, bold key phrases, lists, and no walls of unformatted text.

source.author: Kara Pernice, NN/g
source.work: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web (2017, rev. 2026)
source.quote: The F-shaped scanning pattern is bad for users and businesses.

prefers: Use prominent headings with information-rich opening words
Bold key phrases; employ lists and bullets
Remove unnecessary content
forbids: Leave walls of unstructured text
Let headings fail to out-rank body text visually
Let visual weight contradict importance

measure.what: Heading font-size and weight monotonic with level (h1 ≥ h2 ≥ h3 ≥ body); longest paragraph in words; ratio of headings and list items to total text blocks.
measure.mustFail: h2 rendered at 14 px regular while body is 16 px; 400-word paragraphs, no lists.
measure.mustPass: h2 at 24 px semibold, paragraphs ≤ 80 words, one list.

exceptions: The pattern needs moderate, not high, interest — highly motivated readers read
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Dashboards read numbers and charts more than prose, and admin tools and transaction screens carry less body text to scan.

viewpoints.claim: Cut word count by half: no happy-talk intros, no instruction paragraphs before forms, no marketese, sentence case everywhere.

source.author: Jakob Nielsen
source.work: How Users Read on the Web (1997)
source.quote: People rarely read Web pages word by word; instead, they scan the page

prefers: Reduce word count by half compared to traditional writing
Limit paragraphs to one idea each
Use sentence case everywhere except proper nouns
forbids: Open with welcome or happy talk
Put instruction paragraphs before forms
Use promotional language ('marketese')
Set labels in ALL CAPS or Title Case

measure.what: Word count between a form's heading and its first input; word count of blocks starting 'Welcome' or 'Thank you for'; buttons and labels in all caps or Title Case; sentence count in instructions.
measure.mustFail: A 120-word paragraph explaining how to fill a 3-field form.
measure.mustPass: Heading, three labelled fields and one hint.

exceptions: Nielsen also asks for outbound links to build trust — brevity is not zero text
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Long-form docs and product descriptions legitimately carry more prose than the brevity rule assumes.

viewpoints.claim: Work the way the sites and platforms users already know; a convention beats a locally optimised novelty.

source.author: Jakob Nielsen
source.work: OK-Cancel or Cancel-OK? (2008)
source.quote: Following platform conventions is more important than optimizing an individual dialog box.

prefers: Keep button order identical in every dialog
Highlight the most common button as default, except for dangerous actions
Prefer descriptive labels over 'OK'
Let users keep a familiar version for a while when changing
forbids: Invent a new pattern for a solved problem
Vary the same control's placement between screens

measure.what: Logo in header links home; a search input has type=search or a search label; primary/secondary button order is the same in every dialog; cart and account icons stay where they were on other screens.
measure.mustFail: Two dialogs on one site with opposite Cancel/Confirm order.
measure.mustPass: Identical order everywhere.

exceptions: Desktop apps follow their own OS: Windows OK-first, Apple OK-last
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Dashboards follow fewer platform-wide conventions than pages built from standard chrome; a stripped-down transaction flow may carry none of that chrome to check.

viewpoints.claim: Make targets big, space them apart, and put them where the pointer already is; touch targets at least 1 cm square.

source.author: Aurora Harley, NN/g
source.work: Touch Targets on Touchscreens (2019)
source.quote: at least 1cm × 1cm (0.4in x 0.4in)

prefers: Make targets big
Give icons labels so the label extends the target
Keep ample spacing between targets
Put the call to action near the final form fields
forbids: Pack icon-only 24 px controls edge to edge on touch layouts
Crowd targets

measure.what: Bounding box of each interactive element at the mobile viewport (1 cm ≈ 38 CSS px; 24/44 px are the usual proxies); centre-to-centre spacing; distance from last input to submit; label inside the clickable box.
measure.mustFail: 20×20 px icon buttons 4 px apart.
measure.mustPass: 44×44 px hit areas, 8 px gap.

exceptions: Infinite targets along screen edges for mouse — size matters less at an edge
Primary CTAs, moving users, children and the elderly need larger than the minimum

viewpoints.claim: Fewer equal-weight choices at a decision point, with one recommended; but never use seven as a cap on menu length.

source.author: Jon Yablonski (Laws of UX)
source.work: Hick's Law — Laws of UX
source.quote: The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices.

prefers: Minimise choices when response time is critical
Highlight a recommended option
Keep longer menus if the alternative is abstract labels
forbids: Offer many equal-weight primary actions at one decision point
Use the 'magical number seven' to justify design limits
Simplify to the point of abstraction

measure.what: Count same-weight primary actions in a view; count options in a select or radio group with no recommended default. A menu's item count alone is not a failure.
measure.mustFail: A pricing page with 6 plans, none highlighted, 6 identical 'Choose' buttons.
measure.mustPass: Same 6 plans, one marked 'Recommended' with the only filled button.

exceptions: Recognition, not recall, governs menus — length is a scan cost, not a memory cost (Nielsen)
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Reading content has no timed decision point to reduce choices at; dashboards and admin tools present choices but rarely under time pressure.

viewpoints.claim: Polish makes a screen look more usable than it is; discount your aesthetic impression and run the measurable checks first.

source.author: Kate Moran, NN/g
source.work: The Aesthetic-Usability Effect (2024, rev. 2026)
source.quote: Users' tendency to perceive attractive products as more usable. People tend to believe that things that look better will work better — even if they aren't actually more effective or efficient.

prefers: Rate your own screen after the measurable checks, not before
Treat polish as tolerance for minor problems only
forbids: Read polish as usability
Let an attractive surface hide a usability problem

measure.what: Did the evaluator judge the screen usable because it looks good? Re-check the verdict against the count-kind entries before trusting it; 'attractive' is the variable and stays taste.

exceptions: With severe usability issues, or functionality sacrificed for aesthetics, users lose patience

viewpoints.claim: Accept every reasonable form of an input — spaces, dashes, case, whitespace — and normalise it, instead of rejecting it.

source.author: Jon Yablonski (Laws of UX)
source.work: Postel's Law — Laws of UX
source.quote: Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send.

prefers: Accept variable input and translate it to your format
Normalise on blur
Define boundaries and give clear feedback
forbids: Reject spaces or dashes in card or phone numbers
Reject leading or trailing whitespace in email
Treat email as case-sensitive
Force a date format the field could parse

measure.what: Drive each formatted field with equivalent variants ('4111 1111 1111 1111' vs '4111111111111111', ' a@b.co ', '+44 20…' vs '02…') and compare validation outcomes.
measure.mustFail: A card field shows an error for spaces.
measure.mustPass: Same value accepted and normalised on blur.

exceptions: Inputs where ambiguity is dangerous, such as dates in medical or legal contexts
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages take no formatted input; dashboards and catalogue pages take little beyond a search or promo box.

viewpoints.claim: One visually distinct primary action per view, left-aligned with the form, and distinguished by more than colour.

source.author: GOV.UK Design System
source.work: Button component
source.quote: Avoid using multiple default buttons on a single page. Having more than one main call to action reduces their impact, and makes it harder for users to know what to do next.

prefers: Make key actions visually distinctive
Use restraint so emphases do not compete
Align the primary button to the left edge of the form
Highlight the default, except for dangerous actions
forbids: Put two or more filled primary buttons in one view
Signal emphasis by colour alone

measure.what: Cluster interactive elements by computed background, border and weight; the most emphatic cluster per view must have one member; primary's left edge aligns with the inputs; emphasis differs in weight, fill or border, not colour only.
measure.mustFail: 'Save' and 'Cancel' both solid brand-colour buttons.
measure.mustPass: 'Save' filled, 'Cancel' as a text link.

exceptions: Do not pre-highlight a dangerous action as the default (Nielsen)
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Docs pages and dashboards often carry no single primary action to emphasise.

viewpoints.claim: In flows of three or more steps give some sense of position; do not assume a step bar helps — GOV.UK removed one with no effect.

source.author: Jon Yablonski (Laws of UX)
source.work: Goal-Gradient Effect — Laws of UX
source.quote: The tendency to approach a goal increases with proximity to the goal.

prefers: Show a step or position label in long flows
Update the position between steps
forbids: Leave a long wizard with no step label anywhere
Cite the Zeigarnik effect as the reason for a progress bar
Fake progress to manipulate

measure.what: Presence of a step or position element in flows with 3 or more steps, and whether it updates between steps.
measure.mustFail: A 6-step wizard with no step label anywhere.
measure.mustPass: 'Step 2 of 6' or a heading that changes each step.

exceptions: Short flows — GOV.UK's own guidance omits indicators by default
Artificial 'endowed progress' edges toward manipulation — flag, do not recommend
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Only multi-step flows have a position to show; marketing, content, data and shop screens are single views, admin only when it runs a setup wizard.

viewpoints.claim: End every journey on a reachable confirmation with a next step, never on an error, a blank page or a dead end.

source.author: Jon Yablonski (Laws of UX)
source.work: Peak-End Rule — Laws of UX
source.quote: People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end, rather than the total sum or average of every moment of the experience.

prefers: Design the final moment of the journey deliberately
Give the terminal state a confirmation and an onward link
forbids: End a flow on an error
End a flow on a blank page
End a flow on a dead end with no next step

measure.what: After the final action: a confirmation screen or status exists, is reachable, has at least one onward link and no error state.
measure.mustFail: Form submit returns to the same page with fields cleared and no message.
measure.mustPass: 'Application sent — reference ABC123. What happens next…' with a link.

viewpoints.kindsWhy: Dashboards and reading content have no terminal state; a marketing, admin or shop task ends well only when its action hands off to a flow elsewhere.

viewpoints.claim: Keep essential content and the primary action in the main column, styled like content, never in a right rail, top strip or animated coloured box.

source.author: Kara Pernice, NN/g
source.work: Banner Blindness Revisited (2018)
source.quote: Users have learned to ignore content that resembles ads, is close to ads, or appears in locations traditionally dedicated to ads.

prefers: Put essential content in the main column
Style key notices like content
forbids: Put the primary CTA in the right rail or a top banner strip
Give a key notice animation, coloured background or fancy formatting
Place essential content next to real ads

measure.what: Is the journey's primary action or a required notice positioned in the right rail (x > 70% of desktop viewport) or in a full-width top strip with background fill and animation?
measure.mustFail: 'Complete your profile' only as an animated right-rail card.
measure.mustPass: Same prompt inline in the main column on a plain background.

exceptions: On mobile, large inline ads do get fixated — the effect is weaker for inline placement
viewpoints.kindsWhy: A one-thing-per-page transaction screen, and dense admin and dashboard layouts, carry less of a rail or banner strip in which to misplace content.

viewpoints.claim: Every input has a visible label outside the field; placeholder text is never the label, the hint or the only format example.

source.author: Katie Sherwin, NN/g
source.work: Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful (2014)
source.quote: Disappearing placeholder text strains users' short-term memory.

prefers: Give every text input a visible label
Put hints outside empty form fields
forbids: Use placeholder text in place of a label
Use placeholder text for hints or examples
Hide the label visually and rely on the placeholder

measure.what: Any input or textarea with a placeholder and no visible associated label, or with a visually hidden label; placeholder used as the only format example.
measure.mustFail: <input placeholder="Email"> with no label.
measure.mustPass: <label for=e>Email</label><input id=e>.

exceptions: A single-field search where the button label carries the meaning is the usual carve-out; the fetched page states none explicitly
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing, content, dashboard and catalogue pages carry at most a search or email field.

viewpoints.claim: Stack the label above its field, left edges aligned, a few pixels apart, so label and field are read in one fixation.

source.author: Marieke McCloskey, NN/g
source.work: Form Design Quick Fix: Group Form Elements Effectively Using White Space (2013)
source.quote: users can see the text field in the same fixation as the label

prefers: Top-align labels for familiar data like names, addresses and payment
Let users move in one direction: downward
forbids: Put left labels far from their fields
Use right-justified labels with a ragged left edge
Put the label inside the field

measure.what: For each label/input pair: label box bottom ≤ input box top and label left edge ≈ input left edge within a few px; if side by side, the gap between label right edge and input left edge.
measure.mustFail: Right-aligned labels in a 200 px column, inputs in a second column, 24 px gap.
measure.mustPass: Labels stacked above inputs, 4–8 px gap.

exceptions: Landscape phones: switch to left-aligned to keep the field visible above the keyboard (Baymard)
Left-aligned is acceptable when labels are of similar length and as close to the fields as possible (NN/g)
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages carry no labelled fields; dashboards and catalogue pages carry few.

viewpoints.claim: Forms run in one vertical column; only coherent entities like city/state/ZIP or card/expiry/CVV share a row.

source.author: Baymard Institute
source.work: Form Field Usability: Avoid Extensive Multicolumn Layouts (2023)
source.quote: Use a single-column layout to support users' visual understanding of forms

prefers: Keep one vertical path through the form
Allow a shared row only for a single coherent entity
forbids: Lay out two independent question columns

measure.what: Cluster inputs by left x-coordinate; more than one column of independent inputs, not in the same fieldset or an allowed coherent row, fails.
measure.mustFail: Name and email in column 1, phone and company in column 2.
measure.mustPass: All four stacked, with expiry and CVV side by side.

exceptions: Coherent-entity rows: city/state/ZIP and card number/expiry/security code
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages carry no multi-field forms; dashboards and catalogue pages rarely have one with more than a field or two, and expert admin tools may intentionally use denser multi-column layouts for speed.

viewpoints.claim: Size each input to the data it expects: short boxes for year, postcode and CVV; one consistent width for variable data like email.

source.author: Jamie Holst, Baymard Institute
source.work: Form Field Usability: Matching User Expectations (2010)
source.quote: Matching your customer's expectations – even when it comes to the subconscious expectations of how wide an input field should be – is crucial.

prefers: Fit fixed-length data with a width that matches it
Give variable common data one consistent width
forbids: Make a CVV box as wide as an address line
Let a card-number field visibly truncate

measure.what: Rendered input width in ch of its font versus maxlength, inputmode, autocomplete token or pattern length: cc-csc wider than ~8 ch, postal-code at full width, or email narrower than ~20 ch.
measure.mustFail: CVV input at 100% width.
measure.mustPass: CVV at 5 ch, card number at 22 ch.

exceptions: Full-width inputs on narrow phones are the norm — check at desktop widths or compare relative widths within the form
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages carry no typed inputs of known length; dashboards and catalogue pages carry few.

viewpoints.claim: Validate a hard field after the user leaves it, never on focus or while typing, and clear the error live once it is fixed.

source.author: Luke Wroblewski with Etre
source.work: Inline Validation in Web Forms (A List Apart #291, 2009)
source.quote: 22% increase in success rates … 42% decrease in completion times … 47% decrease in eye fixations

prefers: Validate on blur or when the input reaches its expected length
Re-check on each keystroke once an error shows and clear it when fixed
Keep success and error messages visible rather than fading
Reserve inline validation for hard fields like username and password
forbids: Validate before and while typing
Show an error on focus of an empty field
Validate only on submit

measure.what: Drive a field: focus shows no error; typing an invalid value shows none (unless length threshold reached); blur shows an error adjacent via aria-describedby; typing a fix clears it without blur.
measure.mustFail: Error text renders the moment the field receives focus.
measure.mustPass: Error only after blur, cleared on the corrected keystroke.

exceptions: Simple fields need none; premature validation was worse than none (Wroblewski)
viewpoints.kindsWhy: Marketing and content pages carry no hard fields worth validating inline; dashboards and catalogue pages rarely do either.

viewpoints.claim: Count fields, not steps: a guest checkout needs about eight, with optional fields collapsed behind links and billing defaulted to shipping.

source.author: Baymard Institute
source.work: Checkout Optimization: minimize form fields (2024)
source.quote: The number of form fields in a checkout impacts overall usability far more than the number of steps.

prefers: Consolidate to a single 'Full Name' field
Hide Address Line 2 and the coupon field behind links
Default billing to shipping
Offer account creation after purchase
forbids: Count steps as the metric
Show every optional field by default

measure.what: Count visible input, select and textarea across the checkout (excluding hidden and collapsed); optional fields shown expanded; separate first/last name fields; an open coupon field.
measure.mustFail: 14 visible fields including Address Line 2, Company, coupon and two address blocks.
measure.mustPass: 8 fields with 'Add address line 2' and 'Have a coupon?' as disclosure links.

exceptions: Regulatory or fraud fields that genuinely cannot be defaulted
The minimum of 8 assumes a standard guest checkout
viewpoints.kindsWhy: The count is calibrated on checkout and sign-up, which are transaction screens; it transfers loosely to admin create-record forms and not at all to marketing, content, data or shop screens, which are not checkouts.

viewpoints.claim: Split a public-facing form so each page asks one question, decision or piece of information, with eligibility questions first.

source.author: GOV.UK Service Manual
source.work: Structuring forms (2018)
source.quote: Start by splitting the form across multiple pages with each page containing just one thing

prefers: Ask one question per page
Start with questions that reveal ineligibility
Branch so people answer only relevant questions
Break complex tasks into smaller steps
forbids: Put a long multi-section form in a public-facing transactional service

measure.what: Count distinct questions (label groups or fieldsets) per page in a flow; count required inputs per page.
measure.mustFail: One page with 9 unrelated questions.
measure.mustPass: 9 pages, one question each, with a check-answers page.

exceptions: Be consistent, not uniform: internal expert tools and repeat users may prefer denser pages
viewpoints.kindsWhy: The rule is for public transactional flows; the other five kinds are not structured as a sequence of one-question pages.

viewpoints.claim: Name the actor and their need before drawing a screen, then let measured behaviour, not hunches or looks, decide what changes.

source.author: GDS / GOV.UK
source.work: Government Design Principles, principles 1, 3 and 4
source.quote: Service design starts with identifying user needs. If you don't know what the user needs are, you won't build the right thing.

prefers: State the actor and need before the screen
Measure real behaviour
Start small and iterate
forbids: Design to a hunch
Design to an aesthetic

measure.what: Does the journey name its actor and need (uxcli context show), and is the design decision traceable to observed behaviour rather than a hunch or a look?
